opus-5.5.text:
I think AI is quietly changing the economics behind a lot of outsourcing decisions, and I'm not sure everyone has fully absorbed that yet.

For a long time, the logic was simple: if you have a large volume of work, say writing a lot of code, processing documents, or handling customer support tickets, you could get it done more cheaply by hiring a big team in a lower-cost region. Labor arbitrage made sense because the work scaled roughly linearly with headcount.

What I'm seeing now, especially in software engineering, is that a small team of really skilled people using AI coding assistants can sometimes match or beat the output of a much larger team. When one engineer with good tools can do the work that used to take several, the math changes. Coordination costs start to dominate. Managing a large distributed team means handoffs, specs, time zones, and miscommunication. A small, tight team that sits close to the product and the customer can iterate much faster.

There's also a shift in where the bottleneck is. When writing code gets cheaper, the scarce resource becomes deciding *what* to build: product judgment, understanding the user, writing a clear spec. That work is hard to outsource because it needs deep context. So I think we'll see some work that used to go offshore move back closer to the core team, not because labor got cheaper there, but because you need fewer people and you want them close to decision-making.

I don't want to overstate it, though. Outsourcing won't disappear. Many outsourcing firms are smart and are adopting AI themselves, so they'll become more productive too. The firms that thrive will probably be the ones that stop selling hours and headcount and start selling outcomes, using AI to deliver more per person. The ones that just compete on low hourly rates for routine tasks are going to feel real pressure.

My advice for engineers anywhere in the world is the same: learn to use these AI tools really well. The productivity gap between someone who's fluent with AI and someone who isn't is getting large, and that matters more than geography.

r001.rationale: The response says a small team of skilled people using AI coding assistants can match or beat a much larger team, directly raising the stated possibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more interesting shifts that's happening, and I don't think most people have fully internalized it yet.

For a long time, the logic of outsourcing was pretty straightforward. If you had a big body of work, say a lot of software to write or a lot of customer support tickets to handle, the economics pushed you toward finding a large team somewhere where labor is cheaper. You trade off some coordination cost, some communication overhead, maybe some quality variance, in exchange for lower cost per unit of output. And that trade was often worth it.

What AI assistance does is change the leverage of a single skilled person. If one engineer with good AI coding tools can now do what used to take a team of five or ten, then a lot of the reason you went out and assembled that big team in the first place starts to go away. You don't need to coordinate across time zones or write detailed specs for a team you've never met. You just have a small group of people who understand the problem deeply and are very productive.

I've seen this in some of the teams I work with. Small teams, sometimes just a handful of people, are shipping things that a few years ago would have required a much larger headcount. And the quality is often higher, because there are fewer handoffs and the people doing the work actually understand the context.

So my sense is that the appeal of outsourcing to large, lower-cost teams goes down, at least for a lot of knowledge work. The value shifts toward people who have genuine expertise and taste, and who know how to direct these tools well. If you're outsourcing work that's fairly routine, that's exactly the work AI is getting good at, so the cost advantage of a large team shrinks pretty quickly.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think this means outsourcing disappears. There are still a lot of tasks where you need people, and there are still lots of talented engineers all over the world. But I think the model changes. Instead of hiring a hundred people to execute a spec, you might hire five really good people anywhere in the world, give them great tools, and get a better result. Geography matters less, and raw headcount matters less. What matters more is skill and judgment.

And honestly, I think that's a good thing for a lot of individual workers, because it means someone in any country who learns to use these tools well can be extraordinarily productive and compete on quality rather than just on cost. The playing field in some ways gets more level, even as the old volume-based outsourcing model gets less attractive.

r001.rationale: The response says a small group using AI tools can do work that once required five or ten people, and that five skilled people with great tools may get a better result than hiring a hundred to execute a spec.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could change the economics of outsourcing quite a bit. If a small team with AI assistance can do what previously required a much larger team, then the advantage of having access to lots of lower-cost labor becomes less important. And the coordination overhead—communicating requirements, handing work off, checking the results—can become a larger fraction of the total cost.

But I don't think that means outsourcing disappears. Those teams can use AI too. The interesting question is who can use it to deliver a better outcome, rather than simply offer more hours of labor at a lower price. You might see smaller, highly capable teams competing with much larger organizations, regardless of where they're located.

r001.rationale: The response says a small AI-assisted team can do work that previously required a much larger team, reducing the advantage of lower-cost labor, and notes that smaller, highly capable teams could compete with much larger organizations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could change the economics of outsourcing quite a bit. If a small team with AI assistance can do the work that previously required a much larger team, then the cost of labor per person becomes less important. What matters more is how effectively that team uses AI, how well they understand the task, and how quickly they can iterate.

There’s also a coordination cost to having a large team. You have to communicate requirements, hand work off, review it, and get corrections back. If AI lets a smaller team do more of that work directly, you may save on both labor and coordination.

But I wouldn’t conclude that outsourcing goes away. Those teams have access to AI too. An outsourcing company that learns to use these tools well could become much more competitive. So I think the advantage shifts from simply having access to lower-cost labor toward being able to deliver a good outcome quickly with AI.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI-assisted small team could do work that previously required a much larger team, with the advantage depending on how effectively the team uses AI and understands the task. This conveys the possibility of a capable small team outperforming a larger, lower-cost team.
